stops.name: The open Ocean: the double reckoning begins
stops.campa: On the ninth of September the last land sinks astern, and men who have sailed all their lives weep to watch it go. That same day the Admiral opens his second ledger: henceforth he will keep two reckonings, a true one for himself and a shorter one for the crew, so the leagues will not frighten them. The doctored log is the first fiction written about America. The trade wind takes the ships like a hand in the small of the back: day after day fair, following, relentless, and the men begin to whisper: what wind will ever blow us home?
stops.quote: He decided to count fewer leagues than they made, so that if the voyage were long the people would not be frightened and lose heart.

stops.name: The Sargasso Sea: April in Seville
stops.campa: The ships enter a sea no Christian has written of: meadows of yellow-green weed stretching to every horizon, so thick the men fear shoals in mid-ocean and heave the lead: no bottom at two hundred fathoms. A live crab rides the weed; the Admiral keeps it, arguing land. Tunny play, a river-bird passes, the dew falls sweet. He writes that the mornings are a delight, that nothing is wanting but the song of nightingales. The crews read the weed as a snare set for ships; he reads it as a garden path, and logs the omens like a man collecting rents.
stops.quote: The air was very soft, like April in Seville, so that it was a pleasure to be in it, so fragrant it was.

stops.name: The false landfall: Gloria in excelsis at sunset
stops.campa: At sunset Martín Alonso Pinzón climbs the Pinta's poop and cries land, land, and claims the reward, a blue rampart in the southwest that every man aboard swears to. The Admiral falls to his knees and gives thanks; the crews of all three ships sing Gloria in excelsis Deo, and men go up the rigging to see the new world in the last light. At dawn there is nothing: cloud, built by longing into mountains. The ships sail on through the hole in the horizon where an island had stood all night in ninety imaginations.

stops.name: The eve of mutiny
stops.campa: Thirty-one days from La Gomera, farther west than any keel in the memory of the sea, the men can bear no more. They gather in the waist of the Santa María and say it aloud: turn back, or we are dead men, and some say quieter things about a foreigner and a dark night and the sea that tells no tales. The tradition adds the pact of the Pinzóns: three days more, and if no land, come about. The Admiral cajoles, promises, stands like iron: he has come to go to the Indies, and with the help of Our Lord he will go until he finds them.
stops.quote: He told them that, however much they complained, it was useless; he had come to go to the Indies, and so he would continue until he found them, with the help of Our Lord.

stops.name: The night of the light
stops.campa: The wind blows harder than at any hour of the voyage, the sea runs, and the ships race west through the dark at their greatest speed, land-signs thick around them: a green branch, a carved stick, a berry-laden bough. At ten in the night the Admiral, standing on the sterncastle, sees a light to the west: small, like a wax candle rising and falling, as of a torch in a fisherman's boat. Pedro Gutiérrez sees it too. It shows, and hides, and shows. Four hours later the Pinta's gun speaks. The canon gives the first light of America to his eyes, and the ten thousand maravedís with it.
stops.quote: A light, like a little wax candle that rose and lifted.

stops.name: Guanahaní: the landing at San Salvador
stops.campa: At dawn on Friday the twelfth of October the boats go in through the reef of an island the Lucayans call Guanahaní. The Admiral steps ashore bearing the royal standard, the captains Pinzón beside him with the green cross banners; he kneels, weeps, kisses the ground, and names the island San Salvador, Holy Savior, taking possession with notary and witnesses as the people of the island gather, naked and beautiful and unafraid, wading out with parrots and skeins of cotton to trade for hawk-bells and red caps. Two worlds stand on one beach, each believing the other has fallen from the sky.
stops.quote: They all go as naked as their mothers bore them... They should be good servants and quick of understanding, and I believe they would easily become Christians, for it seemed to me they had no religion.

stops.name: The naming chain: Concepción, Fernandina, Isabela
stops.campa: Through the Lucayan shallows he sails from island to island, laying names on the world like a man christening his own children: Santa María de la Concepción for the Virgin, Fernandina for the King, Isabela for the Queen: heaven first, then the crowns. Guides taken from Guanahaní pilot him and learn Castilian words; every islander points onward and south when gold is shown, saying Colba, Cuba. He notes harbors that would hold all the ships of Christendom, fish painted like roosters, air like May. The ledger of Paradise fills page by page.

stops.name: Cuba: Bahía de Bariay, Cipango sought
stops.campa: He enters a river-mouth on the coast of a land so great the guides cannot say where it ends, and he needs no persuading: this is Cipango, or the mainland of the Great Khan itself. He names it Juana for the Prince. Palms unlike Guinea's or Castile's, mountains like Sicily's, dogs that never bark, the song of crickets all night; he writes that he could stay forever. The grass grows down to the waterline, and the Admiral of the Ocean Sea, anchored off a fishing hamlet, composes the most repeated sentence of praise in the canon of discovery.
stops.quote: It is the most beautiful land that human eyes have ever seen.

stops.name: Río de Mares: the embassy to the Khan, the drinkers of smoke
stops.campa: From the harbor he names Río de Mares he dispatches an embassy inland to the court of the Great Khan: Luis de Torres, who has Hebrew, Chaldean and some Arabic, the converso interpreter carried across the Ocean to greet the Orient in the tongues of Zion, and the seaman Rodrigo de Jerez. They find no Khan: a village of fifty palm houses, and men and women walking with firebrands of rolled leaf, drinking the smoke of an herb they call tabacos. The first Old World lungs fill with tobacco. Days later Pinzón and the Pinta crowd sail and vanish east, gold-hungry, the fleet's first treason.

stops.name: Hispaniola: the Spanish Isle
stops.campa: On St Nicholas's day he crosses the Windward Passage and enters a harbor he names Puerto de San Nicolás, on an island the people call Haití and Bohío. Its vegas and mountains so recall Castile that he names it La Isla Española. Here the people are fairer, the cotton finer, and the gold at last real: leaves and grains of it, traded from a place inland they call Cibao, which the Admiral hears, with perfect conviction, as Cipango. The cacique Guacanagarí sends him a belt with a mask of beaten gold. Every day the log promises the sovereigns the source is near.

stops.name: Christmas night: the wreck of the Santa María, La Navidad built
stops.campa: In the calm of Christmas Eve, the Admiral asleep, the helm left to a ship's boy, the Santa María settles onto a coral bank and will not come off. Guacanagarí weeps at the news, sends every canoe of his people, and not a lace-point is stolen. From her timbers Columbus builds a tower and fort and reads the wreck as God's own instruction: the flagship was to become the first town, and he names it La Navidad for the night of its death and birth. Thirty-nine men volunteer to stay with the gold country before them. The first Christian settlement of the New World is made of shipwreck.
stops.quote: Our Lord had caused the ship to run aground there so that a settlement might be founded there.

stops.name: The Gulf of Arrows: first blood at Samaná
stops.campa: Homeward along the coast, the Pinta returned, Pinzón's excuses swallowed for the voyage's sake, the ships water in a bay where men with long hair and blackened faces carry great bows of yew-like wood. A trade sours; the Ciguayos rush the shore party with cords and arrows and take the first Spanish steel in reply. Two are wounded; the rest flee. The Admiral names it Golfo de las Flechas, the Gulf of the Arrows, and notes in the log, believing these to be the man-eating Caribs, that the first skirmish of two worlds has been fought. Then he turns the bows northeast, for Spain, into winter.
